functions.name: Sign in
functions.description: Operators and security admins sign in through the corporate SSO. The portal sends the token with every API call.

functions.name: Request a certificate
functions.description: An operator or an internal service submits a certificate signing request. The certificate service stores it.

functions.name: Approve a request
functions.description: A security admin approves or rejects a pending request.

functions.name: Issue a certificate
functions.description: After approval, the key service signs the certificate with the CA signing key. The certificate is stored with the request.

functions.name: Download a certificate
functions.description: An operator or an internal service downloads an issued certificate and its chain.

functions.name: Revoke a certificate
functions.description: A security admin revokes a certificate and records the reason.

functions.name: Publish the revocation list
functions.description: Every hour the CRL publisher builds the revocation list and writes it to the revocation list bucket. Relying services download it through the CDN.

functions.name: Send expiry reminders
functions.description: Every day the certificate service finds certificates expiring within 30 days and emails the owning team.

functions.name: Rotate the CA signing key
functions.description: A security admin starts a rotation. A new key version is created and used for new certificates.

functions.name: View audit history
functions.description: A security admin views who requested, approved, issued and revoked each certificate.

functions.name: Deploy a new version
functions.description: The deploy pipeline builds a new container image and rolls it out to the cluster.

assumptions.text: The load balancer is reachable from the internet, so it is a second entry point next to the API gateway, until the client confirms otherwise.
The CDN is reachable from the internet. It serves the portal pages and the revocation list.

The assessed environment is production. The written answers describe the dev environment and are assumed to hold for production, because the client says production follows the same design. Nothing is shared between dev and production until the client answers.
The cloud provider protects the inside of its managed services: key management, secrets store, database, storage, CDN, logging and audit trail.
The cache holds certificate data until the client says what it holds.
Nothing checks that requests reaching the certificate service come from the API gateway.

scope_decisions.reason: Operators are people who use the portal. They are shown as users, not broken down.
Security admins are people who use the portal. Their access path through the API gateway is inside the assessment.
Internal services are other company systems that call the portal. The link and the client certificate they use are inside the assessment.
The answers say the corporate SSO is run by central IT and used by other company applications. The token check on the API gateway is inside the assessment.
It is deployed in the portal's account and serves the portal pages and the revocation list.
It is in the portal's account and holds the portal web pages.
It is in the portal's account and holds the revocation list.
It is in the portal's account and builds the revocation list.
It is the documented public entry point of the portal.
It checks the sign-in token on every request.
It is in the portal's network and the diagram shows it reachable from the internet.
It is part of the portal's network.
It is the portal network's route to the internet.
It is the configuration of the portal's own network.
It is the portal's own service and handles all certificate requests.
It is the portal's own service and signs certificates.
It is in the portal's network, next to the certificate service.
It holds all certificate requests, issued certificates and the audit history.
The key is the portal's CA signing key. The cloud provider runs the key service; the key policy the platform team sets is inside the assessment.
It holds the portal's database password and notification API key.

It is part of the build and release chain, outside the portal, even though it sits in the portal's account. The image pull into the portal's services, and what the services accept, are inside the assessment.
It records API calls in the portal's account.
It holds the portal's application logs and metrics.
It is an outside service. The link to it, the data sent and the API key the portal holds are inside the assessment.
It is in the portal's private network and passes requests from the gateway and the internet-facing load balancer to the services.
It is part of the build and release chain, outside the portal. The deploy into the portal and the deploy role it uses are inside the assessment.

questions.text: Is the API gateway a service your cloud provider runs, or something your team installed and runs itself?
questions.why_it_matters: If your team runs it, everything inside it is part of the assessment, not only its settings.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Run by the cloud provider; only its settings are assessed

questions.text: Does the load balancer do anything with requests, such as checking sign-in, filtering or ending encrypted connections, or does it only pass them on?
questions.why_it_matters: If it acts on requests, it needs the same attention as the API gateway.

questions.text: What data does the cache hold? Does it include certificates, keys or sign-in tokens?
questions.why_it_matters: The cache is in the diagram but no document describes it, so its protection needs are unknown.

questions.text: Is the cache a service your cloud provider runs, or something your team installed and runs itself?
questions.why_it_matters: If your team runs it, its software and settings are part of the assessment.

questions.text: Who decides who can read the certificate database and who changes its settings?
questions.why_it_matters: The database holds every certificate request and the audit history.

questions.text: Can the portal UI bucket be reached directly from the internet, or only through the CDN?
questions.why_it_matters: Direct access would let anyone read or, with a wrong setting, change the portal pages.

questions.text: Can the revocation list bucket be reached directly from the internet, or only through the CDN?
questions.why_it_matters: Anyone who can change the revocation list can make revoked certificates look valid.

questions.text: Who decides who can read the secrets store and who changes its settings?
questions.why_it_matters: The secrets store holds the database password and the notification API key.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Only the portal services and the platform team

questions.topic: who can read or delete the records
questions.text: Who can read or delete the audit trail records?
questions.why_it_matters: Anyone who can delete audit records can hide changes to the portal.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Only the platform team, recorded as an assumption

questions.topic: who can read or delete the logs
questions.text: Who can read or delete the application logs?
questions.why_it_matters: Logs can show certificate requests and errors; deleting them hides activity.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Only the platform team, recorded as an assumption

questions.text: Where does the pipeline keep the credentials for the deploy role?
questions.why_it_matters: Whoever holds these credentials can deploy any code to the portal.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Kept in the hosted CI service's secret settings

questions.text: Do security admins use company-managed computers to reach the portal?
questions.why_it_matters: Admins can approve and revoke certificates and rotate the CA signing key.

questions.topic: who uses it and from which devices
questions.text: From which devices do operators use the portal?
questions.why_it_matters: Personal devices would widen who could misuse a signed-in session.

questions.topic: authentication between gateway and certificate service
questions.text: How does the certificate service check that a request really comes from the API gateway?
questions.why_it_matters: Without a check, anything inside the network could request certificates.
questions.default_if_unanswered: No check, recorded as an assumption

questions.topic: authentication between load balancer and certificate service
questions.text: Does the certificate service check the sign-in token on requests that arrive through the internet-facing load balancer?
questions.why_it_matters: If not, a public load balancer is a way around the gateway's sign-in check.
questions.default_if_unanswered: No check, recorded as an assumption

questions.text: Do the dev and production environments share cloud accounts, keys, databases or credentials?
questions.why_it_matters: The answers describe dev and the diagram describes production. Anything they share lets a weakness in dev reach production certificates.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Nothing is shared, recorded as an assumption

questions.text: Is the corporate SSO used only by the portal, or also by other company applications?
questions.why_it_matters: A shared sign-in stays outside the assessment; a dedicated one is inside.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Shared company sign-in, treated as an interface

questions.text: Is the portal's cloud account used only by the portal, or also by other systems?
questions.why_it_matters: In a shared account, only the portal's own resources are part of the assessment.

questions.text: Can the API gateway be reached from the internet, or only from inside the network?
questions.why_it_matters: An internet-facing gateway is an entry point.

rationale.title: The internet-facing load balancer is treated as a second way in

rationale.title: Who can read or delete the audit records is not documented
